en: A Collection of Divergent Meanings from Master Suí’s *Commentary on the Śrīmālā-sūtra*, compiled by the Disciple of Tiantai, Qiànshū. The preface states:

Regarding the three [aspects] within the general category of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), the intention of the *Commentary* author is easy to understand. However, the Master [Suí] says: "Regarding the three realms..."
There are three [realms] which are the objects of cessation; that is, the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) serves as one. There is one which is the agent of cessation;

because it has previously cultivated the outflow-free state in succession and emerged from the prisons of the three realms, the three realms are used as the three [objects], and the outflow-free as the one. Combined, these constitute four.
The subsequent statement, "One sūtra and one teaching are thus," refers back to the *Sadāprarudita* [Sūtra] and others as recorded therein.
The Master’s intention is that the *Sadāprarudita* and other such works merely establish a single aspect of the *Avataṃsaka*; therefore, he says, "One teaching is thus."
Regarding the statement "the same applies to other sūtras," the commentary says: "There are still many sūtras that have not been cited. The Master’s intention was not that;
rather, he simply meant those various sūtras cited below.

Regarding the doubt raised by the questioner: since they have heard similar statements in other sutras mentioned above, they request that [the Master] cite them, saying, "I wish to hear the authentic proof.

Next, regarding the exclusion of what is not [the path], the *Ji* (Commentary) states: "First the mind, then the path. The Master’s intention is that this merely sets forth both the chapters on the Mind and the Path.
Section on the Gate. How is this known? According to the subsequent explanation of the ten minds, it is stated in each case that one "arouses the mind and practices the Way.
Judging by this, we know there is no distinction between them.

Regarding the statement that "next, or first, one gives rise to this mind, and subsequently gives rise to non-mind," the commentary states: "This is *buddhatā* (enlightenment); 'non' refers to the ten negations (*daśa-naiḥsvabhāvya*).
The Master’s intention is that "this" refers to the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), while "non" refers to the nine negations. How is this known?
It is verified by the subsequent statement that "both 'is' and 'non' are excluded. Thus it is understood.
Regarding the two sections within the [mouth-mountain] (*khāṃ*): the intent of the record is as follows. The first section concerns the relative nature of "is" and "is not.

"Is" refers to *bodhi*; "is not" refers to the ten negations. The second section concerns the internal and external; that is, the two vehicles are considered "external," while the nine negations constitute the two extremes.

Although this is a preliminary analysis, there remains a concern that the former treats the mind alone, whereas the latter treats both mind and objects. The Master’s intention states that the former...

However, regarding the ten [perfections], they are equal as both internal and external; this is the application of the subsequent sequence. The latter refers to the mind in relation to the ten, not merely to their selection.
That is to say, it is not [limited to] bodhi alone.
Regarding the establishment of the name within the "Twenty-five Dharmas": the intention of recording this is likely to provisionally include the subsequent section on the "Bonds" (*saṃyojana*).

The Master’s intent is also not without the contemplation of the subsequent section on the "Bonds. According to the meaning of the cited sūtra, it simply reaches as far as the sūtras concerning internal and external observation.
Furthermore, because it concludes there, we know that this [section] is also established as a name based on the contemplation of [the bonds], as they are combined into a single unit.
At the end of the tenth chapter on "Arising," it concludes by stating that [the stages] ultimately reach the skillful means (*upāya*) of the sages.

This record specifically correlates the two vehicles and bodhisattvas with the three objects (*viṣaya*) in contrast to the perfect skillful means. The Master’s intention is that these are merely the skillful means of their respective teachings and belong only to the stage prior to realization.

Furthermore, this is discussed in terms of the time of initial arousal [of the mind], not yet concerning entry into the [formal] stages; therefore, they are collectively termed "skillful means. The Perfect Teaching universally employs all ten objects.
Regarding "expedient means" (upāya): it is not limited to the two vehicles or bodhisattvas as being expedient means.

As for what is called "expedient means," it refers only to the stage prior to the realization of truth by those of the two vehicles and bodhisattvas; once truth is realized and perfected, it is no longer termed "expedient means," nor is it discussed in terms of its arousal.

Furthermore, in the *Siyiliaojian* (Private Excerpts), it says: "The untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) transform into the aggregates of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā-skandha*). The commentary states: "After cessation, one receives the body of dharma-nature outside the realms;
this is called the 'aggregates of dharma-nature. The Master’s intention is that attaining [this state] while still in this very body is itself the dharma-nature."
This does not depend on [the state] after cessation. Furthermore, it says:

"For one who perceives constantly, 'different thoughts' refers to the severance [of them]. This records that the internal and external stages of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) constitute "different thoughts.
The Sūtra itself explains that these "different thoughts" are eightfold. "Patience" (*kṣānti*) refers to the person; the person is indeed patience. That is the cause.

Furthermore, regarding the subsequent statement that "even the minor faith of Śreṇika cannot be attained," the *Commentary* says: "The meaning of 'minor vehicle' (Hīnayāna) is that it refers merely to a small amount of faith.
Regarding the "arrows and stones," the *Commentary* says: "This can be understood. Some say that when two people were fighting together, one used stones and the other used [arrows].
Regarding the arrow: when they were victorious in battle, each claimed credit for their contribution. Thus, two men disputed over whether it was the arrow or the stone that had achieved the feat.
Furthermore, there was an account concerning the six causes: at one time, a *shuan* bird dropped an arrow eighteen inches long onto the palace of King Wei.

The King ordered his former ministers to deliberate together on the matter. Some claimed it was the arrow; others claimed it was the stone. Thus, the names "arrow" and "stone" arose from such disputes. At that time, there was a man of wisdom...
A person arrived later and said, "There is no need for this dispute. This [bow] comes from the state of Wei. The people of Wei are tall and large, so they used stones as arrows.
Now, do not take the meaning of this; simply take the meaning of the previous dispute."

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "peaceful mental application" within the context of the peaceful mental application of the dharma-practice, it says: "I observe the characteristics of dharmas; yet when observing sleep, it is not eliminated.
One should then explain 'cessation' (śamatha), which possesses great efficacy. [The commentary] does not provide a separate explanation for this record. The Master said:

"Cessation through the five contemplations for settling the mind (pañca-vinodana) is like the concentration of counting breaths (ānāpāna-smṛti). Cessation is like pure water, similar to the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā). Cessation is great loving-kindness (maitrī), similar to compassion (karuṇā)."

Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is the Great Illuminating Mantra; it resembles the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). Quiescence (*śamatha*) is the Buddha; it resembles the contemplation of the Buddha’s mindfulness (*buddhānusmṛti*).
Such is the Master’s intended response. The *Jì* does not provide an explanation.

Furthermore, regarding the statement in the "Examination" (Liaojian) section at the end of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* concerning the "four sets of four," making sixteen gates (*dvāra*), the commentary does not explain it.
The Master’s intention is as follows: the gate of arising (*utpāda-dvāra*) negates all dharmas; the gate of arising establishes all dharmas; the gate of arising both negates and establishes;
and the gate of arising neither negates nor establishes. This applies likewise to the remaining gates up to the gate of cessation (*nirodha-dvāra*). Thus, there are thirty gates in total.

Furthermore, regarding the statement in the *Tri-nirukti* that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are combined and thus called "sentient beings" (*sattva*), this is recorded as evidence for the preceding *dharma-paryāya*.
According to the Master’s intention, this is precisely the *prajñapti-paryāya*. The five aggregates are *dharmas*;
since they are subsumed under *dharma*, sentient beings are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*). Therefore, they belong to the category of designation.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that within the "mutual dependence" (xiāngdài jiǎ) there are three types of provisional constructs (*prajñapti*) and thus no "unborn dharma-object" (*anutpanna-dharmālambana*), the *Jì* (Commentary) states:

"By applying contemplation and investigation within the 'causal formation' (*hetusamutthāna*) and 'continuity' (*saṃtati*), one has already attained the realization of non-arising; because this realization is directed toward [the absence of] such an object, it is called the 'unborn dharma-object.
However, the Master’s intention is not so. Rather, within mutual dependence itself there are inherently three types of provisional constructs. As for the term "unborn dharma-object," it refers to...
That is to say, the three unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are the objects of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Furthermore, considering the provisional middle [view]: from the point where the greed of the lower realms becomes light until it reaches non-greed? The commentary states: "Among those many instances, only one is cited;

therefore, it is called 'one instance'. The Master’s intention is that the phrase "one instance" below represents the perspective of the masters of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* in defending the *Abhidharma*.
He said: "Although such an objection may be raised, I fear it would miss the Buddha’s intent. Therefore, he says: 'The Buddha sometimes speaks differently according to specific circumstances;
one should not say that the Abhidharma is entirely incorrect. Thus he asks: 'How can conventional designations be fixed?'"

Furthermore, regarding the statement in the *Pó sī jiǎ zhōng* (The Refutation of the Provisional Nature of Thought) concerning "successive abandonment" (*ānupūrvika-prahāṇa*) and "leaping abandonment" (*vyutkrāntaka-prahāṇa*), the intention of the *Jì* (Commentary) does not cite the Master’s [Vasubandhu’s] view.

It merely identifies the points where these names are applied. As for the specific mention of "successive": when one first employs untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) to abandon the [defilements of the] views, and subsequently abandons five grades of the [defilements of] cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) before entering cessation, one receives the name of a candidate for the stage of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka*). As for "leaping": one first employs mundane wisdom (*laukika-jñāna*).

Having completed the abandonment of the five grades of afflictions of the desire realm through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one subsequently abandons them at the time of seeing [the truths] (*darśanamārga*);
thus it is said that they are "transcended. Because the mundane wisdom (*laukikajñāna*) used to abandon these afflictions is weak, this process is identical to the gradual sequence.
After abandoning the first and second grades, one is called a "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) because of being reborn in several families; subsequent cases follow this same principle.

Furthermore, regarding the "Discrimination of the Transcendent and Non-transcendent" at the end of the *Yingluo* [Sutra], the Master’s intention was to provide proof for the four propositions of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), though the commentary does not mention this.
Moreover, following the five kinds of impurity, within the contemplation on the impermanence of the mind, it says: "When the cage breaks and the bonds are severed, one departs and does not return."

The record states: "Only those who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) are called 'non-returners who have severed the fetters'. However, the Master’s intention is that one is called a "non-returner who has severed the fetters" simply upon the end of a single lifetime;
thus it says, "the seal is broken and the inscription is formed."
Furthermore, among the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), the remaining five are not explicitly mentioned; they are merely summarized.
The *Record* simply states that they are subsumed within "wisdom" (*prajñā*) and "unfailing liberation" (*avipraṇāśa-vimukti*). This is merely a rough correspondence.

According to the Master’s intention, following the *Dharmadhātu-krama*, he takes the constant illumination of the three periods of time as the minds of the three types of sentient beings, and he preaches the Dharma without needing to observe them for even a moment.
To have no divergent thoughts is to not lose one's prior mindfulness; this constitutes the non-diminution of wisdom. The remainder is as stated in the text.

Regarding the phrase "establishing the doctrine for the morning court," the intent of the record is that while various treatises merely rely on their own specific teachings, the *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation) universally encompasses all four teachings.
The Master’s intention was not otherwise; rather, it concerns the extent of the doctrinal schools shared by the sutras and the treatises. This original source intends...

Upon returning to my native country, I departed in haste and could not be exhaustive in detail. Fearing that my considerations might not have been all-encompassing, there may be slight discrepancies between this record and the provisional measures [I previously employed].
Nevertheless, each account has its own clear outline; those who read it later should examine them closely as a mirror for reflection.
The *Shiyao chao* (Scroll I) states: "Furthermore, it says: 'The ten gates transmitted to Japan circulated separately, titled *Guoqing zhiguan*, were recorded by the Upādhyāya.
It also mentions those such as 'the identity [of the three truths]' (*titong*). I do not yet know who this Upādhyāya Zhiguan was.
Was this person deeply versed in the teachings of our own school? Were the original texts he first recorded entirely free of error?"
How can one follow the views of those who have already passed away and take them as the right path, assuming that every practice they established may be relied upon?
For instance, according to the "Divergent Meanings in Master Zhi's *Zhiguan*" recorded by Qian Shu, it treats the three realms as being without outflows (*anāsrava*).

Can one possibly follow all three of these [commentaries] in their entirety? How much less so regarding their various differing interpretations, which specifically contradict the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) and establish their own personal views?

Therefore, they all claim that "the text of the *Jiwen* (Commentary) is easy to understand," citing the Master [Zhiyi] as their authority (*yúnyún*). Furthermore, this master claims to be the Seventh Patriarch.
Therefore, we know that Master Zhizhi was most likely this very teacher. If it were he, then [the text] would be entirely unreliable;
since he was ignorant of Jingxi’s profound intent, there must have been alterations. Furthermore, there are many errors and omissions in the Japanese teachings;
only the separately circulated *Ten Non-dual Gates* is identical to the edition established by [Fengxian] Yuanqing. Others...
Since I have previously sent you the *Zhuzhi* (Pointing at the Pearl) for use in that country, you must certainly rely upon it to verify and transcribe [the text].
Even if it is an old edition, you must cross-check it according to the meaning; do not rely solely on the literal wording.

Zhipan’s narrative states: *Zhìyào* criticizes the heterodox interpretations recorded by the Japanese monk Kanshuku regarding the Master Suí’s *Zhǐguān*, specifically his claim that the three realms constitute the "three" within the general category of the "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).
I have carefully examined this; since Master Suí personally received the *Zhǐguān* from Jingxi, it is impossible for him to have arbitrarily initiated such a theory.
It was likely the private interpretation of Kanshuku and his peers who, under false pretenses, attributed it to him.

Master Suí (Zhiyi) merely practiced it himself; thus we know that the Japanese separately produced the *Ten Non-dual Gates* titled *The National Qingzhong Monastery Upādhyāya’s Zhiguan*, which all the people of that country rely upon as their model. Furthermore, the *Yiyao* states:
"Since he previously sent the *Zhuzhi* to that country, they must have relied upon it for their transcription. Based on this, moreover—
Knowing that the people of the country rely upon and revere what was originally entrusted to them, he composed this text under the name of the Venerable Zhi Guan as a means of transmission.
The words of Siming were intended to refute Qian Shu’s veneration of the original; yet people of the world do not realize this.
This was taken to mean that he was refuting Master Sui [Daoxuan]. I request that this meaning be used as the interpretation.
The *Nihon Hōji Shiki* states: "There is a one-fascicle work titled *Igi* (Divergent Meanings) among the records;
this is the *Igi* extracted by Venerable Dōsui from outside the *Kōketsu*. His disciple Kanshuku heard it and recorded it" (end quote).
